issues.legal_issue: A mandatory compensation formula for acquired property that caps compensation by reference to a remote requisition-date value, without a rational connection to the property's value when acquired, violates the pre-amendment constitutional guarantee of a just equivalent.
material_facts: The land had been requisitioned years before it was acquired, and its acquisition triggered the right to compensation.
The statute required the arbitrator to award the lesser of the property's open-market price on the acquisition date and twice its open-market price on the requisition date.
The arbitrator had no discretion to use the acquisition-date valuation if the requisition-date formula produced a lower amount.
No circumstances or rational basis were shown for using the requisition date to determine the value payable on acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The impugned compensation formula was arbitrary and violated Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood before the Fourth Amendment; the challenged provision was void.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) before the Fourth Amendment, compensation for compulsory acquisition had to be a just equivalent of the property taken. Legislative principles for determining compensation were reviewable to determine whether they accounted for the property's true value. Fixing value at an anterior date with no relevant connection to acquisition was arbitrary. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, and N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector; it distinguished East Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. v. State of Madras because the person to be compensated there could choose among valuation methods. It also held that the phrase “have regard to,” read in context with the mandatory valuation provisions, did not give the arbitrator discretion to disregard the prescribed formula, consistent with Ryots of Garabandho v. Zamindar of Parlakimedi.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: The proceeding challenges the legal basis for determining compensation for property compulsorily acquired.
predicates.mandatory_lower_of_valuation_methods: The decision-maker was required to award the lower amount produced by two prescribed valuation methods and could not select the other method as fairer.
predicates.requisition_date_unrelated_to_acquisitio: The prescribed requisition-date valuation had no demonstrated rational connection to the property's value when it was acquired.

issues.definition: When a compensation challenge concerns compulsory acquisition and a mandatory lower-of-methods formula relies on an unrelated requisition-date value, the formula is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not disturb a lower court's discretionary decision to excuse delay unless the decision rests on a wrong principle, an error of law, or a failure to consider matters requiring consideration.
material_facts: The High Court considered whether delay should bar relief in a constitutional writ proceeding concerning compensation for acquired land.
It found no sufficient delay to refuse relief and stated that, even assuming delay, it would condone it in view of the importance of the issues.
The appellate court was not shown that the High Court had acted on a wrong principle, committed an error of law, or failed to consider relevant matters.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's exercise of discretion concerning delay.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court will not normally interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision unless satisfied that it acted on a wrong principle, committed an error of law, or failed to consider matters demanding consideration. The Court relied on Zacharia v. Republic of Cyprus.

rule.if: appeal_from_discretionary_delay_decision and lower_court_considered_delay and not demonstrated_discretionary_error

predicates.appeal_from_discretionary_delay_decision: The proceeding is an appeal from a lower court's discretionary decision about whether delay should prevent relief.
predicates.lower_court_considered_delay: The lower court considered the delay and decided whether it should bar relief.
predicates.demonstrated_discretionary_error: The appellant demonstrated that the lower court applied a wrong principle, made an error of law, or failed to consider a matter requiring consideration.

issues.definition: On an appeal from a discretionary delay decision, if the lower court considered delay and no discretionary error is demonstrated, the appellate court does not interfere.
